doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

chapter: Working with American visitors and moving to the U.S.
title: Accompanying Americans, New York from 1980, and songwriter albums with Maxine Sullivan
summary: Ingham accompanied Russell, Shavers and Carter, moved to New York in 1980, played with Vic Dickenson and Doc Cheatham, took Richard Rodgers' requests, and made songwriter albums with Maxine Sullivan, meeting Jule Styne and Burton Lane; J. Fred Coots anecdote.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: Yeah. But anyway I did accompany a lot of American artists, Pee Wee Russell, Charlie Shavers, Benny Carter, oh it was so nice. But of course when you come here it’s a different story because this country’s so vast. You know you don’t see these people anymore, wherever. But when they came to England — anyway, Red Allen was so encouraging. But I got here in 1980 and started working in New York. There were still a few clubs going there and I started beating around and working in places. But I was lucky enough to play with some of the greats of the era that I particularly love, like Vic Dickinson and Doc Cheatham, both now gone. I mean there’s very few of those people left, and hardly any of them play, which is so sad. But it’s what happens, it’s just the way things have to be. But I’m very glad I came here because really America is still the source of this music and you find wonderful things and you can still sense the continuity of what you loved and what still goes on. For example I was playing in a restaurant when I first got here, and up comes a note, could you play this song and that song. And I knew these songs, and they were Richard Rogers’ tunes. The guy that sent the note up was Richard Rogers. But at the time he’d lost his voice. He couldn’t speak. He had this problem with the throat cancer or something. So he had to write everything down. And on the way out he wrote a note saying thanks so much for playing my tunes. And of course being British, had I known he was there I wouldn’t have played the Rogers songs, I’d have thought he’s probably sick of hearing that, hearing his own tunes, forget about it. He wanted to hear his own tunes. And they were all like that. And I worked a lot with a wonderful jazz singer, Maxine Sullivan. And I did three albums with Maxine and they were albums devoted to songwriters who were still alive: Burton Lane we did; Harold Arlen we did some songs of the Cotton Club when Harold was still alive; and Jule Styne. And I was so lucky to get to meet these guys, you know. I didn’t meet Arlen, but I met Jule Styne and Burton Lane and to actually meet the songwriters and go to their apartment. And I

remember going up to Jule Styne’s apartment and he gave us the song that he kind of, one of the last songs that he’d written and he said we could use it on the album. And of course, sure we’d love to if we could do it, and we did it. And up in his apartment there were paintings by George Gershwin on the wall. You know Gershwin was a very accomplished artist. And he had one of Gershwin’s paintings. And I remember sitting there and the phone rings, and who’s on the other end of the line is Irving Berlin. So I mean you’re in there and there’s all this thing going on. Irving Berlin, a living legend, talking to Jule Styne who is a legend.

And a Gershwin painting on the wall? That’s not bad. You think New York is a pretty good place to be. You know I love New York anyway. And I met Burton Lane, you know, the great theater composer. You know this whole tradition of the American musical coming out of theater and then going into the movies and then the songs are taken up by bands you know. It’s just a wonderful continuity. And it still lives on in a lesser way. I mean I was playing, and I have a steady gig in New York, I’m lucky to say that because there are so few of them. But I’m playing in this nice little restaurant, and this lady comes in and she said, “do you know a song called ‘You Go To My Head?’” It’s a beautiful tune. So I said sure, so I played it. She says, “my uncle Fred wrote that.” I said, “yeah?” She said yeah there’s a guy called J. Fred Coots who wrote “You Go To My Head” of course and “For All We Know” that beautiful old song, and he also wrote “Santa Claus is Coming To Town” which is his big money spinner you know. So she said, yeah, Uncle Fred, I remember Uncle Fred, she said, every time December came ‘round, he said, “oh we’re going to eat good for the next year” because he got all the royalties on “Santa Claus is Coming to Town.”
Thanks ASCAP, for sending those checks.

ASCAP’s sending those checks in, yeah. And I remember talking to Burton Lane about that, or talking to his wife actually, and she married Burt Lane and she couldn’t figure out how somebody could earn all this money by not going out to work during the day you know. Because all the royalty checks would come in for his songs, like “How About You” and “How Are Things in Glocca Morra,” all those things from “Finian’s Rainbow,” “Ole Devil Moon” — all wonderful songs.
